title: OpenAI says safety is why it won't IPO. Do you buy it?
dek: Altman says going public now is "unwise," citing safety; but at the same time OpenAI is negotiating a $1.2 trillion raise, and the CFO has been excluded from investor meetings.
why: Three Indicators of the Week segments, one number each. The OpenAI segment has real internal tension; the other two are price tracking with average information density.
who: Investors watching AI company governance and IPO timing, and macro observers who want to understand how diesel and fertilizer transmit into food prices.
skip: The show teaser and sponsor read at the top, 0:00-1:00, can be skipped.

points.h: US households paid $820 extra for this war
points.body: Waylon's indicator is $108 billion — the extra fuel cost US consumers have paid since the Iran war began in late February, gasoline plus diesel combined, or about $820 per US household. The number comes from Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab, which tracks it live on its website, with the red figure ticking upward. The method uses the average price over the 30 days before the war as a baseline, then adjusts for seasonal factors — people drive more in summer, demand is higher, prices were supposed to rise anyway. In other words, it's a counterfactual estimate of what oil would cost if this war hadn't happened. Diesel has already broken $6 a gallon, a record.

points.h: Diesel costs land on your Amazon order
points.body: Most Americans don't drive diesel cars, but diesel prices affect them anyway. Trucks, trains, factories and farms all run on diesel, and the extra money paid at those links gets passed through to grocery prices and Amazon packages. Brown's tracker says this explicitly: higher diesel costs mean higher consumer prices, whether or not you fill up. This transmission chain is the key to understanding the fertilizer segment later — diesel and fertilizer together push food prices up.

points.h: OpenAI says no IPO while negotiating $1.2 trillion
points.body: Ricky's indicator is $1.2 trillion, the size of the latest funding round OpenAI is negotiating with private investors, per the Financial Times. At the same time, Sam Altman told Fortune he isn't preparing to take the company public, on the grounds that "given everything that's going on with safety, it would be unwise to go public now." Ricky points out the oddity directly: if the product really is unsafe, why keep building it? Earlier this year The Information reported that Altman and CFO Sarah Fryer disagreed on IPO timing — Altman wanted to go public sooner, Fryer was worried about the company's spending.

points.h: The CFO doesn't report to the CEO, which is unusual
points.body: This is the most concrete information in the whole episode. Fryer does not report to Altman — that kind of relationship between a CEO and a CFO is very unusual. Altman is also said to have excluded Fryer from some meetings with major backers, which is likewise unusual. Separately, OpenAI filed a confidential S1 in June, meaning it disclosed its finances to regulators but not to the public. Ricky's inference: if OpenAI's IPO lands and performs badly, that could be bad news for the entire stock and bond market propped up by the AI growth narrative. And if safety really is the issue, going public means being more transparent about financial health and perhaps safety records — so that's exactly why safety is a worry now.

points.h: Anthropic is still pushing ahead with its own IPO
points.body: Ricky uses a metaphor: OpenAI is like a couple that's been together ten years and still can't decide whether to marry — you're worth a trillion dollars, it's time to grow up. Meanwhile rival Anthropic is still pushing ahead with its own IPO. Waylon chimes in that they're like Goldie Hawn and Kurt Russell — together a long time, raising kids together, never married. The conclusion: as long as OpenAI and Anthropic are happy, they don't need to go public, and they can whenever they want.

points.h: Sulfur went from $170 to $1,100 a ton
points.body: Cooper's indicator is $1,100 — roughly what it costs to buy a metric ton of sulfur. The average price over the past decade was about $170, a rise of about 500%, a whole extra zero. Sulfur is a key input for fertilizer, and fertilizer is essential for growing food. The strange part: the US produces most of its own sulfur, domestic supply is fine, but several other major supply hubs are in the Middle East, China and Russia, all places with obvious tensions. Sulfur also has to pass through major Middle Eastern commercial waterways — Cooper names the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab-el-Mandeb, saying they are being blocked.

points.h: The US produces its own sulfur but can't escape global prices
points.body: This is the oil logic: even if the US is a major producer, it isn't immune to global price increases. Supply falls, and the price gets pushed up for everyone. The scale of the increase has already changed the economics for fertilizer producers — a company called Mosaic told them it has idled two plants in Louisiana because of insufficient sulfur supply. This isn't a forecast, it's an impact that has already happened.

points.h: Diesel plus fertilizer means food inflation rises another 3% to 5%
points.body: Connect the previous two: diesel at record highs plus a fertilizer shortage leaves the agriculture industry in a bad spot. Rabobank, a bank focused on agriculture, expects US food inflation to rise another 3% to 5% next year — after already rising 4% to 6% this year. Cooper says he put that number in this week's Indicator newsletter.
